lines.text: You help a yeti captain unload his orange ship, the Sunny Disposition. He has peel in his fur.
"We owe you one,"
he says.
"Mostly in oranges."
Old Wick, a frogfolk lamplighter, says goodnight to every lamp by name. You carry his ladder. He shows you a secret ledge along the Long Bridge.
"Nobody else looks."
From the lighthouse, you see one thread of gem-light rise toward the mountain. The old merfolk keeper sits up in her bathtub.
"I saw nothing,"
she says. Neither did you.
At the noodle stall, a stone troll named Mortar points at an empty chair.
"Every table keeps one for whoever comes next. Today, that is you."
So, why are you going north?
Mortar stops stirring.
"The gull dropped its fish before the light came. Heard something first."
He has thought about that for three days.
Mortar sets out an extra bowl
"for whoever needs it."
A lost faun gobbles it up, spots her cousins' wagon, and runs after it with the spoon.
Mortar taps your chair.
"Yours now. Everyone here started again."
He gives you bread. At rush prices, that is practically a house.
Mortar points at the Big Bowl.
"Nobody finishes it."
You finish it together.
"Hm,"
says Mortar. From a troll, that is clapping.
On the way to the docks, a selkie family steps off a boat with everything they own.
"Is there room here for selkies?"
asks the grandmother.
"We were told to try the Empty Chair, an inn up the hill."
You find a plaque with a selkie founder on it. The grandmother reads it twice.
"Then we are home."
She gives you her river charm for the road.
The boggart sells rumors in jars. You pay with a button. The rumor inside is:
"The mountain is grumpy."
Then the boggart says it again, slowly, looking west toward the marshes.

There are three roads north. East to Stone Crossing, where the toll is a story. North across the Plains, with the rush wagons. West through the Whispering Marsh, if the frogfolk like you. The fishmonger points up.
"Griffin couriers carry so many letters, they can barely fly."
In the market stands the Griffin Post, a tower full of round windows. Clerks stuff more and more letters into the couriers' sacks. The postmaster, a griffin called Quill, has lost count.
"Hands!"
she squawks.
"Anybody with hands!"
Your griffin and the couriers talk about headwinds. Then they whisper. Since the red night, no courier flies near the mountain.
"The air up there hums,"
says one,
"like a kettle."
A courier you know lands on a chimney and peers at the stone.
"Not mine. That fell out of the sky."
He fluffs his feathers.
"Finders keepers!"
Inside the Empty Chair, a selkie scholar stands on a table.
"The gem-light fell upward!"
Everyone laughs. Two trolls carry her outside, table and all. She just wants someone to believe her.
The scholar hugs you. It is a very wet hug, because she is a selkie.
"Professor Marrow Tidewell,"
she says.
"You are the first to believe me all week!"
She gives you the owl-feather clasp from her coat.
Outside, the scholar draws a gem with eight sides on a napkin. Her soggy notes are signed Professor Tidewell.
"Old stories tell of a seal, like a lid on a jar, made of eight pieces called facets,"
she says.
"I think the mountain just threw seven of them across the realm. The eighth is still inside."
She looks at your glowing pocket.
"Oh! You've got one."
Along the quay, gem-buyers shout prices. The loudest is Madame Coralie Fenn, a merfolk in a barrel on wheels.
"Rush prices, darlings!"
She offers a huge price for your red stone. A pigeon faints. Sell it, or keep it?
You name a bigger number. She names a smaller one. Back and forth you go, until a second pigeon faints. She pays double, and adds a brave whistle
"for cheek, darlings."
Madame Fenn pays you in a clanking purse and adds a lucky bead.
"I never forget a good seller."
The hum rolls away in her barrel.
At the foot of the Outfitters' Steps, a sheeple grocer named Mrs. Tuft has her barge tied up. Her price tags are stuck in her wool.
"One thing for the road, free,"
she says.
"Food, a potion, or a light. Pick one."
The sunbloom potion glows like a tiny sunrise.
"For bumps, scrapes and grumps,"
says Mrs. Tuft.
"Mostly grumps."
The mosslight glows soft and green.
"It likes to be talked to,"
says Mrs. Tuft.
"Not sung to."
Mrs. Tuft takes one look at the red stone, and every jar on her barge rattles.
"Lovely,"
she says, not meaning it. She hands you a honeycake, so you will leave sooner.
Your kitsune points at the next stall.
"Those are bootlaces painted yellow."
Tobble is so grateful he gives you real quickfoot laces.
Tobble stops singing.
"I had a fresh start too,"
he says.
"I used to make boots for a duke."
He sells you laces at last year's price.
Back at the Empty Chair, the innkeeper is a stone troll named Flint, in a nightcap much too small. He has one cupboard bed left, and lots of people want it.
"Earn it,"
he rumbles.
There are three hundred supper bowls. You wash until your fingers wrinkle like raisins. At midnight Flint checks one bowl, says
"Hm,"
and hands you the key.
The selkie family hears your voices and comes thundering down the stairs.
"You'll squash in with us,"
says the grandmother. The room is tiny, but warm.
At dawn you pass Mortar's noodle stall with your bags packed. He stirs one slow turn.
"Going, then."
There is time for one goodbye before the caravans leave.
Mortar stirs one slow turn. Then another.
"Longstride. Lantern wagon. Listens to the whole answer. Tell her Mortar sent you."
That is the most he has said all week.
Mortar ladles out the biggest breakfast of your lives, then pins his apron's thistle on you.
"Strong noodles. Strong legs."
A long stir.
"Come back."
Mortar holds the warm stone to his ear for a long time.
"Sings,"
he says at last.
"Like my grandma's pot, just before it boiled over."
In the caravan yard, a centaur named Hesper Longstride is checking her lantern wagon.
"I have room for one more crew,"
she says.
"Tell me why you want to come."
The Longstride banner is taller than you, and the wind wants it badly. You hold it up anyway.
"Front,"
says Hesper.
"Don't drop it."
"That wagon was robbed twice this week,"
says Hesper. You offer to guard it anyway. She hands you a long pole with a hook.
Hesper's ears swivel.
"Mortar sent you? Mortar hardly talks to anybody."
She nods once. From that troll, a name is as good as a letter.
Hesper hands you a lantern pole.
"Crew,"
she says. The wagons roll toward the North Gate.
"Cargo, then,"
says Hesper, kindly. You ride with the turnips. One sits in your lap like a cat. The wagons roll toward the North Gate.
A big bell called the Leaving Bell hangs over the North Gate. Past it are green fields and, far away, Mount Red Sky.
"Say goodbye however you like,"
says Hesper.
You wave, and the Exchange waves back. Tobble sings goodbye, three keys too high. Madame Fenn's barrel rolls along beside you.
"Bring me something shiny, darlings!"
There is Professor Tidewell, running beside the wagons.
"Count every stone you see!"
she shouts.
"Write it down!"
She throws you her napkin drawing, trips over a goose, and keeps waving.
Mrs. Tuft has a tray of jars for the top of the Outfitters' Steps, and you help carry it. The pickle jar rattles all the way up. At the top she counts them.
"Good hands,"
she says.
On the way, a lantern pole snags a washing line. You hold the pole steady while Hesper unhooks it. Long underwear floats down onto a goat. Then Hesper hands you the pole, lantern and all.
"Keep it,"
she says.
"Steady hands should carry their own light. On to the North Gate."
Your thornguard plants both boots by the lantern wagon. A pickpocket takes one look and leaves.
"Steady,"
says Hesper, and hands over a long pole with a hook.
